narrative:
The law school’s decision is based on a model predicting your chance of failing the bar exam on the first attempt. That risk stands at 59.6 percent, meaning you are more likely to fail than pass, which is why your application was denied. Three factors drove this outcome, arranged by influence.

The most powerful factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 3.30, it is just above the 3.23 average for admitted students, yet the model still treated it as a serious warning sign. In the model’s eyes, this GPA disproportionately pushes you toward bar failure, perhaps because it expects a stronger academic foundation for the rigors of law school. The second most important factor, your third-year class rank, worked in your favor. Placing in the ninth decile, far above the 5.79 average, signals that you performed strongly in your later coursework, and this was the only major element pulling you toward passing. Unfortunately, that positive signal was not enough. Your LSAT score of 40, while above the 37.18 average, also leaned the prediction further toward failure, making it the third-most influential factor. Although your score is respectable, the model appears to view it as still too low to compensate for the GPA risk.

What should you do next? Focus on addressing the strongest risk factor. Consider retaking the LSAT to achieve a significantly higher score, or if possible, take additional undergraduate courses to raise your GPA before reapplying. Your strength in later academic years is valuable, so build on that record. A year of strengthened preparation could tip the probability in your favor.
